claims.text: A post-fabrication oxidation treatment can produce a thin, continuous B2O3 passivation layer on a boride surface.
A thin, continuous B2O3 layer will reduce molten-aluminum attack on boride-based components.
As-fabricated boride components have microstructural boundaries and surface defects that can initiate molten-aluminum corrosion.
Oxidation at approximately 600 °C for 1 hour in air or controlled oxygen, followed by rapid cooling, will form a thin, adherent B2O3 surface layer.
The oxidation temperature must be high enough to promote B2O3 scale formation but below the temperature at which the boride phase melts or destabilizes.
Approximately 660 °C represents a typical molten-aluminum process exposure temperature.
The oxidation treatment will create a continuous and uniform B2O3 passivation layer.
The B2O3 layer will fill microstructural defects and cover active sites on the boride substrate.
The B2O3 scale acts as a diffusion barrier to molten aluminum.
The B2O3 scale reduces direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride.
The passivating layer suppresses aluminum infiltration and chemical attack at grain boundaries and defect sites.
Pre-oxidized boride samples will have lower molten-aluminum corrosion rates than untreated samples under identical exposure conditions.
Pre-oxidation will reduce weight loss or corrosion penetration depth by at least 30% relative to the untreated baseline.
Effectiveness depends on optimizing oxidation temperature, time, and oxygen availability to obtain a continuous B2O3 layer.
Nonoptimal oxidation conditions could cause incomplete passivation or damage to the boride structure.
The intervention is most applicable to components having a uniform, well-controlled boride microstructure.
The long-term adhesion and stability of the oxide under repeated thermal cycling and prolonged molten-aluminum exposure are uncertain.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement may vary with microstructure and plating-process conditions.
